Arrival.notes: Shown before the timed talk. Twelve content slides, about eight minutes. Click, or press →, to drive in.

Construction and Infrastructure.notes: Our sector is Construction and Infrastructure. A stadium buys civil works, materials, building systems and specialist expertise. We use the 2034 stadium programme, with King Salman Stadium as our main example. The Ministry of Sport procures its works and Populous is the designer. FIFA’s 2024 bid baseline assessed fifteen stadiums across five cities. Construction generated 7.8 percent of Saudi value added in 2023. We ask how this public spending can leave Saudi firms able to supply the next project.

Who buys, who supplies.notes: Our sector is construction and infrastructure. In 2023 Saudi construction produced SAR 646 billion of output and SAR 338 billion of value added, which is 7.8% of all value added in the economy. The 2034 World Cup adds fifteen stadiums in five cities. Our case is King Salman Stadium in Riyadh, the largest, with 92,760 planned seats. The buyers are public: the Ministry of Sport for King Salman, Qiddiya Investment Company and Aramco for other venues. The suppliers are joint ventures of international and Saudi contractors, plus specialist firms for mechanical systems and facades. So who supplies matters: every package bought from abroad is money that leaves the Kingdom.

The spending multiplier.notes:
The spending multiplier starts when one payment becomes income for someone else. A stadium contractor pays workers and suppliers. They spend some of that income again, creating later production. Imports and saving reduce the next round. A GDP multiplier compares additional GDP with additional public spending. If an extra one hundred million riyals causes one hundred and twenty million in extra GDP, the multiplier is one point two. That is only a teaching example. A company choosing a Saudi supplier is a microeconomic decision. The combined effect on GDP is macroeconomics. EP credit up to six belongs to a different calculation.

Qualification: the 100m / 120m example illustrates the definition only. GDP is incremental value added over a specified period, compared with the baseline. Imports, capacity, price changes and policy responses can reduce the effect.

Construction and Saudi GDP.notes:
Our sector is construction and infrastructure. GASTAT reports six hundred and forty-five point eight billion riyals of construction output in 2023. Subtract three hundred and seven point five billion of bought-in inputs, and construction adds three hundred and thirty-eight point three billion of value. That is seven point eight percent of Saudi gross value added. GDP counts the extra value created in each Saudi stage once. Our academy can help qualified Saudi suppliers win orders, but the GDP effect depends on additional production, imported inputs, capacity and cost. Local invoices alone do not measure a GDP multiplier.

Qualification: 645.8 minus 307.5 equals 338.3bn, using rounded figures. Total Saudi gross value added is 4,332.9bn, so construction is 7.8%. The 52.4% accounting share is not a local-content score or a spending multiplier.

How import-dependent it is.notes:
Start with what construction buys: SAR 307.5 billion of inputs in 2023. Based on GASTAT, 19.7%, SAR 60.5 billion, is imported and 80.3% is made in Saudi Arabia — roughly one riyal in five. How import-dependent is construction? Among the inputs construction buys in volume, two stand out. More than half of the basic metals supplied in Saudi Arabia are imported, 54.5%, and half of the electrical machinery, 50.3%. Cement, glass and basic chemicals are mostly made here. These are national ratios: based on GASTAT, if we assume a stadium is built with the same input mix as Saudi construction, these are the inputs where it depends most on imports. A stadium is likely heavier in electrical and mechanical systems than the average building, so the real dependence may be higher.

Amount = construction use of the product (sheet 6.2 col. H) × its national import rate: basic metals 21.9 × 54.5% = 12.0; electrical machinery 4.0 × 50.3% = 2.0; other chemical products 31.1 × 43.2% = 13.4.

A SAR 4.5bn stadium scenario.notes: We apply the mechanism to a clearly labelled stadium scenario. The group assumes a value of four-and-a-half billion riyals, using other stadium contracts only as scale comparisons. GASTAT’s construction ratios imply about 2,143 million in intermediate purchases. The model estimates 1,721 million in domestic purchases and 421 million in imports. Local suppliers can spend their receipts again. The imports are the first purchase leakage. This is a first-round purchase split, not a measured total multiplier or all the value that stays in Saudi Arabia.

The materials behind the leakage.notes: The chart now names the materials we mean. Protective coatings, sealants and adhesives sit within the chemicals group. Steel, aluminium and copper sit within the metals group. The largest modelled groups are ninety-four million and eighty-three million riyals, together forty-two percent of estimated imports. The amounts still describe whole statistical groups, not item-level invoices. We must confirm the exact grade, quantity, origin and price from supplier schedules. That lets the academy qualify a Saudi substitute rather than simply promise to localise all metals.

Stadium EPP at 20%.notes:
We use the 2026 consultation framework requested for this assessment. Our SAR 4.5 billion stadium scenario has about 421 million riyals of estimated imports, which falls in the second band, 300 to 500 million, at twenty percent. That creates about eighty-four million riyals of required EP credit. We assume the stadium is one main contract awarded to one company, so the whole import value counts toward a single obligation. The first band, 75 to 300 million, is twenty-five percent, and above 500 million it is fifteen percent. The credit factor can reach six only for qualifying activities: a technology-transfer factor of four plus an approved bonus of two. Our proposal must earn that higher value through usable rights and new capability. Six is not a spending multiplier or a promised investment return.

Qualification: 421 × 20% = 84.2m, rounded to 84m. This applies the tier rate to the whole import value; the draft summaries do not say whether tiers are marginal. If marginal: 300 × 25% + 121 × 20% = 99.2m. The 421m covers modelled intermediate-input imports only, so imported equipment or foreign services could raise the EP base.

London 2012.notes: London 2012 shows that a fixed-event construction programme can support a skills legacy. The UK government reported more than three thousand training places and four hundred and eight apprentices. Training connected people to live construction work. The weakness was relying on encouragement rather than binding skills requirements. Our adaptation puts paid practice, independent tests and trainer return into the delivery agreement. We measure what participants can do and where they work afterwards.

The controls.notes: The solution has to pass five tests. It must add capability beyond ordinary warranty training. The IP agreement must actually allow Saudi teams to use the tools and train others. Each supplier keeps its own approved obligation and credit record. Joint purchasing must preserve competition, quality and access for smaller suppliers. Finally, train before commissioning and confirm the next paid placement. We test skills at the start and completion, then check work and trainer return after six and twelve months. We stop or redesign a track that fails these tests.

One academy, three functions.notes:
We propose one shared EP programme for eligible stadium vendors, subject to LCGPA approval. Vendors jointly support one academy with funding, trainers, equipment and licensed know-how. One qualified host runs training and material qualification. The authorised buyer coordinates competitive purchasing. Each vendor retains its own obligation and ledger, and each activity is credited once. Shared delivery reduces duplication and preserves capability for later projects and exports.

Extended: first, suppliers license technical manuals and diagnostic access, provide training equipment, and train Saudi trainers through paid site practice. Second, the hub tests and qualifies specified Saudi coatings, metal products and other materials against the project standard. Existing Saudi manufacturing evidence makes that plausible, but grades and capacity still need checking. Third, the authorised buyer coordinates standard specifications and competitive call-off orders across confirmed sites. This can improve negotiating power without guaranteeing discounts. Later, Saudi-owned training content and licensed services can be sold abroad within the agreed IP rights.

Hands-on training first.notes:
We start with hands-on training at real construction sites, hosted by an existing qualified provider. Before intake, employers must confirm paid placements, a skills gap and next-site work. We also need an affordable budget, usable technical rights, equipment and approvals. Supplier mentors teach practical tasks, independent assessors test skills and future Saudi trainers practise teaching. Only proven results and continuing employer demand justify repeat cohorts or a permanent academy. If jobs, rights or costs do not pass the test, we pause or redesign.

On-slide addition: the proposal is a joint EP delivery programme across participating eligible vendors. Obtain approval before committing shared delivery. Each company keeps its individual obligation and approved activity/cost records. Do not treat all fifteen venues as one legal tender or assume cross-company credit transfer.

Detail for questions: the 24 learners, six trainer candidates and two eligible sites are proposed design targets, not committed places or guaranteed jobs. At completion check independent practical tests, teaching ability, qualified material grades and full delivered costs. At 6 and 12 months verify paid work, return-to-train activity and repeat local orders. If pass conditions fail, reduce the cohort, renegotiate, redesign or stop.

Value now and after opening.notes: The value goes beyond attendance certificates. During construction, qualified Saudi teams perform defined work, local manufacturers can win approved orders, and the buyer can compare consolidated offers with the original price and full delivery cost. After handover, graduates return as trainers, work on the next contracted site and help suppliers sell new services or materials. Later exports could include Saudi-owned courses, licensed commissioning services and qualified products. These are proposed benefits. We verify orders, invoices, competence, repeat work and export receipts separately. The forty-four million assumes the two largest import groups, chemicals and metals, worth 177 million, go to one company, and a quarter of that shifts to Saudi supply. The illustrative forty-four million in extra domestic purchases is not GDP or a promised academy return.

The decision.notes: We ask LCGPA to approve a pilot with clearly allocated supplier activities and evidence for any higher credit factor. The authorised buyer should approve a competitive shared purchasing process with separate contracts and fair supplier access. Our proposed starting design is twenty-four learners at two confirmed eligible sites, with six candidates returning as trainers. These are targets to agree, not results already achieved. To cover the SAR 84 million EP obligation, we plan about 36 million of approved activity: 12 million each on technology transfer at a factor of 3, knowledge transfer at 2 and localisation at 2. These factors are our group assumptions within the draft policy ranges, subject to LCGPA approval; they are not an official scoring formula. At the low end of every range we would need about 63 million, still below 84. Expand only when skills, paid demand, licensed rights, supplier quality and costs justify it. The goal is a Saudi capability that keeps working after the stadium opens.

Thank you.notes: Closing. Thank the audience and invite questions. The four source pages follow in the appendix (press M).
